name: False report (investigator)
officialTitle: FALSE REPORT TO PEACE OFFICER, FEDERAL SPECIAL INVESTIGATOR, LAW ENFORCEMENT EMPLOYEE, CORRECTIONS OFFICER, OR JAILER.
conduct: With intent to deceive, knowingly making a false statement material to a criminal investigation to a peace officer or federal special investigator who is conducting the criminal investigation. The recipient must have the specified official role and be conducting the investigation. An innocent mistake, a merely irrelevant falsehood, or silence alone does not satisfy these stated elements. The actor’s intent to deceive is separate from knowing the statement is false.
penalty: Class B misdemeanor: ordinarily up to 180 days in jail, a fine up to $2,000, or both. The ordinary Class B grade is not changed merely because the investigation concerns a felony. Qualifying repeat-offender findings require separate analysis. The 2011 H.B. 3423 text expressly covers federal special investigators and authorized agency employees; the 2019 addition of corrections officers/jailers did not first create the other recipient branches. Earlier conduct requires the law then applicable.

name: False report (agency employee)
officialTitle: FALSE REPORT TO PEACE OFFICER, FEDERAL SPECIAL INVESTIGATOR, LAW ENFORCEMENT EMPLOYEE, CORRECTIONS OFFICER, OR JAILER.
conduct: With intent to deceive, knowingly making a false statement material to a criminal investigation to an employee of a law enforcement agency authorized by that agency to conduct the criminal investigation. The actor must know the employee is conducting that investigation; employment at the agency alone is not enough. An innocent mistake, a merely irrelevant falsehood, or silence alone does not satisfy these stated elements. The actor’s intent to deceive is separate from knowing the statement is false.

Earlier conduct requires the law then applicable.

name: False report (corrections jailer)
officialTitle: FALSE REPORT TO PEACE OFFICER, FEDERAL SPECIAL INVESTIGATOR, LAW ENFORCEMENT EMPLOYEE, CORRECTIONS OFFICER, OR JAILER.
conduct: With intent to deceive, knowingly making a false statement material to a criminal investigation to a corrections officer or jailer. Unlike (a)(1) and (a)(2), this subdivision does not itself add a requirement that the recipient be conducting the investigation. The false statement must still be material to a criminal investigation. An innocent mistake, a merely irrelevant falsehood, or silence alone does not satisfy these stated elements. The actor’s intent to deceive is separate from knowing the statement is false.
penalty: Class B misdemeanor: ordinarily up to 180 days in jail, a fine up to $2,000, or both. The ordinary Class B grade is not changed merely because the investigation concerns a felony. Qualifying repeat-offender findings require separate analysis. The corrections-officer/jailer branch was added effective September 1, 2019 by S.B. 405; if any element predates that date, earlier law governs.

name: Bail jumping and failure to appear (ordinary)
officialTitle: BAIL JUMPING AND FAILURE TO APPEAR.
conduct: After being lawfully released from custody, with or without bail, on a condition of subsequently appearing, intentionally or knowingly failing to appear according to the terms of that release. A missed date alone does not establish the lawful-release condition, its terms or the required mental state. The offense requiring the appearance is neither punishable by fine only nor classified as a felony. It is a defense that the appearance was incident to community supervision, parole or an intermittent sentence. A reasonable excuse for the failure to appear is also a statutory defense.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. The grade follows the classification of the offense requiring appearance, not a blanket felony label for every missed date. The statute was renumbered from former §38.11 and amended effective September 1, 1994; this is not an assertion that bail jumping was first criminalized in 1994. Earlier conduct requires its applicable law. Bond forfeiture, release conditions and any other charges are separate questions.

name: Bail jumping and failure to appear (fine only)
officialTitle: BAIL JUMPING AND FAILURE TO APPEAR.
conduct: After being lawfully released from custody, with or without bail, on a condition of subsequently appearing, intentionally or knowingly failing to appear according to the terms of that release. penalty: Class C misdemeanor: ordinarily a fine up to $500, with no jail term as the ordinary punishment. name: Tampering with governmental record (false entry; ordinary)
conduct: Knowingly making a false entry in, or false alteration of, a governmental record. An ordinary governmental record within §37.01(2)(A) or (B), with no intent to defraud or harm another. This excludes all special record types in (c)(2)–(6) and (d). This choice excludes the special school/PEIMS records, student-residency enrollment records, contingency-interest appraisal, specified ballot-application information, temporary tags and motor-vehicle financial-responsibility records in §37.10(c)(2)(A), (c)(3)–(6) and (d), except for the expressly described issued-document portion of (c)(2)(A) when selected. A record combining multiple special predicates requires separate grading analysis. It is a defense under (f) that the false entry or information could have no effect on the government’s purpose for requiring the record; this defense is not automatically extended to the other conduct subdivisions.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. The ordinary Class A/state-jail and issued-document third-/second-degree distinction predates the latest 2023 amendment; a current section-version date is not the first effective date of each grade. Earlier conduct requires the applicable historical law; where the retained enactment uses an any-element transition, an element before its effective date invokes the earlier law. Other repeat-offender or sentencing findings require separate analysis and are not presumed.

name: Tampering with governmental record (false entry; issued document)
conduct: Knowingly making a false entry in, or false alteration of, a governmental record. A license, certificate, permit, seal, title, letter of patent or similar document issued by government, another state or the United States, with no intent to defraud or harm another. This scope does not include the school/PEIMS portion of (c)(2)(A), foreign-government documents or other special record predicates. This choice excludes the special school/PEIMS records, student-residency enrollment records, contingency-interest appraisal, specified ballot-application information, temporary tags and motor-vehicle financial-responsibility records in §37.10(c)(2)(A), (c)(3)–(6) and (d), except for the expressly described issued-document portion of (c)(2)(A) when selected. A record combining multiple special predicates requires separate grading analysis. It is a defense under (f) that the false entry or information could have no effect on the government’s purpose for requiring the record; this defense is not automatically extended to the other conduct subdivisions. Subsection (g) creates a presumption concerning intent to defraud or harm for two or more of the same type of specified government-issued records or blank forms. penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. name: Tampering with governmental record (fabricate present use; ordinary)
conduct: Making, presenting or using any record, document or thing with knowledge of its falsity AND intent that it be taken as a genuine governmental record. The apparent-government-record intent is required in addition to knowledge of falsity. An ordinary governmental record within §37.01(2)(A) or (B), with no intent to defraud or harm another. This excludes all special record types in (c)(2)–(6) and (d). This choice excludes the special school/PEIMS records, student-residency enrollment records, contingency-interest appraisal, specified ballot-application information, temporary tags and motor-vehicle financial-responsibility records in §37.10(c)(2)(A), (c)(3)–(6) and (d), except for the expressly described issued-document portion of (c)(2)(A) when selected. A record combining multiple special predicates requires separate grading analysis. It is a defense under (f) that the false entry or information could have no effect on the government’s purpose for requiring the record; this defense is not automatically extended to the other conduct subdivisions. Under (j), a disclaimer such as “NOT A GOVERNMENT DOCUMENT” is not a defense unless it is diagonally printed clearly and indelibly on BOTH front and back in solid red capital letters at least one-quarter inch high. That statutory qualification is not a general promise that a labeled false document is lawful.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. The ordinary Class A/state-jail and issued-document third-/second-degree distinction predates the latest 2023 amendment; a current section-version date is not the first effective date of each grade. Earlier conduct requires the applicable historical law; where the retained enactment uses an any-element transition, an element before its effective date invokes the earlier law. Other repeat-offender or sentencing findings require separate analysis and are not presumed. The disclaimer-format rule in (j) was added effective September 1, 2009; it is not backdated to earlier conduct.

name: Tampering with governmental record (destroy conceal impair; ordinary)
conduct: Intentionally destroying, concealing, removing or otherwise impairing the verity, legibility or availability of a governmental record. Mere careless handling is not the stated intentional conduct. An ordinary governmental record within §37.01(2)(A) or (B), with no intent to defraud or harm another. This excludes all special record types in (c)(2)–(6) and (d). This choice excludes the special school/PEIMS records, student-residency enrollment records, contingency-interest appraisal, specified ballot-application information, temporary tags and motor-vehicle financial-responsibility records in §37.10(c)(2)(A), (c)(3)–(6) and (d), except for the expressly described issued-document portion of (c)(2)(A) when selected. A record combining multiple special predicates requires separate grading analysis. Subsection (b) excepts destruction pursuant to legal authorization and the specific §441.204 transfer of lieutenant-governor records. For local records, legal authorization includes the applicable Local Government Code retention/destruction rules; known litigation or a pending public-records request can prohibit destruction despite an otherwise expired retention period. An ordinary office instruction alone does not establish legal authorization.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. The ordinary Class A/state-jail and issued-document third-/second-degree distinction predates the latest 2023 amendment; a current section-version date is not the first effective date of each grade. Earlier conduct requires the applicable historical law; where the retained enactment uses an any-element transition, an element before its effective date invokes the earlier law. Other repeat-offender or sentencing findings require separate analysis and are not presumed.

name: Tampering with governmental record (destroy conceal impair; issued document)

Mere careless handling is not the stated intentional conduct. A license, certificate, permit, seal, title, letter of patent or similar document issued by government, another state or the United States, with no intent to defraud or harm another. This scope does not include the school/PEIMS portion of (c)(2)(A), foreign-government documents or other special record predicates. This choice excludes the special school/PEIMS records, student-residency enrollment records, contingency-interest appraisal, specified ballot-application information, temporary tags and motor-vehicle financial-responsibility records in §37.10(c)(2)(A), (c)(3)–(6) and (d), except for the expressly described issued-document portion of (c)(2)(A) when selected. name: Tampering with governmental record (destroy conceal impair; expert report)
